source_text: Videamus nunc, an sicut naturae et causae argumenta virgini quoque competere monstravimus, ita etiam disciplinae ecclesiasticae praescripta de muliere in virginem spectant. Non permittitur mulieri in ecclesia loqui, sed nec docere, nec tinguere, nec offerre, nec ullius virilis muneris, nedum sacerdotalis officii sortem sibi vindicare. Quaeramus, an aliquid horum virgini liceat. Si virgini non licet, sed in omnibus eadem condicione subicitur, et necessitas humilitatis cum muliere censetur, unde illi unum hoc licebit quod omni feminae non licet? Quid praerogativae meretur adversus condicionem suam, si qua virgo est, et carnem suam sanctificare proposuit? Idcirco velaminis venia fit illi, ut in ecclesiam notabilis et insignis introeat, ut honorem sanctitatis in libertate capitis ostendat? Potuit Potuit dignius honorari aliqua praerogativa virilis aut gradus aut officii. Plane scio alicubi virginem in viduatu ab annis nondum viginti collocatam. Cui si quid refrigerii debuerat episcopus, aliter utique salvo respectu disciplinae praestare potuisset, ne tale nunc miraculum, ne dixerim monstrum, in ecclesia denotaretur, virgo vidua, hoc quidem portentuosior, quod nec qua vidua caput texit, utrumque se negans, et virginem, quae vidua deputetur, et viduam, quae virgo dicatur. Sed ea auctoritate illic sedet intecta qua et virgo, ad quam sedem praeter annos sexaginta non tantum univirae, id est nuptae, aliquando eliguntur, sed et matres, et quidem educatrices filiorum, scilicet ut experimentis omnium affectuum structae et facile norint ceteras et consilio et solatio iuvare, et ut nihilominus ea decucurrerint per quae femina probari potest. Adeo nihil virgini ad honorem de loco permissum est.
thought_title: No privilege of place or office for virgins
orientation: Tertullian has shown that nature and the reasons for veiling apply to virgins; he now turns to church discipline, asking whether any of the things forbidden to women are allowed to virgins.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see now, whether just as we have shown that the arguments of nature and of cause also apply to a virgin, so also the prescriptions of church discipline about a woman look toward a virgin. It is not permitted to a woman to speak in church, but neither to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer, nor to claim for herself the lot of any manly function, much less of priestly office. Let us ask, whether any of these things is allowed to a virgin. If it is not allowed to a virgin, but she is subjected in all things under the same condition, and the necessity of humility is reckoned with a woman, whence will this one thing be allowed to her which is not allowed to every female? What of prerogative does she deserve against her own condition, if she is a virgin, and has proposed to sanctify her own flesh? Is the pardon of a veil given to her for this, that she may enter into the church notable and distinguished, that she may show the honor of sanctity in the freedom of her head? She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office. Certainly I know somewhere a virgin placed in widowhood from years not yet twenty. To whom if the bishop had owed any refreshment, he could have provided it otherwise at any rate with respect for discipline preserved, lest such a miracle now, I should not say monster, be marked out in the church, a virgin widow, this indeed more portentous, because not even as a widow has she covered her head, denying herself both, both a virgin, who is reckoned a widow, and a widow, who is called a virgin. But she sits there unveiled by that authority by which also a virgin, to which seat besides sixty years not only once-married women, that is married women, are sometimes chosen, but also mothers, and indeed rearers of children, evidently so that built up by experiences of all affections they may easily know how to help other women both by counsel and by comfort, and so that they may have run through those things through which a female can be proved. So nothing is permitted to a virgin for honor from place.

choices.term: nec ullius virilis muneris, nedum sacerdotalis officii sortem sibi vindicare
choices.english: nor to claim for herself the lot of any manly function, much less of priestly office
choices.why: Keeps the legal force of 'vindicare' (claim as one's right) and the climactic 'nedum' (much less), preserving Tertullian's rhetorical escalation from general male functions to priestly office.
rejected: nor to seize any manly function, let alone priestly office
nor to claim any male duty, not to mention priestly office

choices.why: Renders the phrase literally to preserve the idea that subjection is a binding condition of lowliness shared with all women.
Keeps 'venia' as 'pardon' or 'indulgence' to convey Tertullian's sarcastic framing: being allowed to go unveiled is a concession, not a right.

choices.english: in the freedom of her head
choices.why: Preserves the literal phrase 'freedom of the head' which Tertullian uses ironically for the unveiled head, echoing the earlier argument about head covering.
rejected: in the liberty of her head

choices.term: ne tale nunc miraculum, ne dixerim monstrum, in ecclesia denotaretur
choices.english: so that such a miracle, I should not say monster, would not be marked out in the church
choices.why: Keeps the self-correction 'ne dixerim' (I should not say) and the vivid 'denotaretur' (marked out, branded) to preserve Tertullian's rhetorical shock.
rejected: so that such a wonder, not to say monstrosity, would not be pointed out in church
lest such a miracle, I won't say monster, be noted in the church

choices.english: built up by experiences of all affections
choices.why: Renders 'structae' as 'built up' to keep the architectural metaphor of character formed through life experiences, and 'affectuum' as 'affections' to include both emotions and family bonds.
rejected: formed by the trials of all feelings
constructed by experiences of every affection

pass_b_english: Let us now see whether, just as we have shown that the arguments from nature and from causes apply to the virgin as well, the rules of church discipline about women also look to the virgin. A woman is not permitted to speak in church, nor to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer the Eucharist, nor to claim for herself the lot of any manly function, much less of priestly office. Let us ask whether any of these things is allowed to a virgin. If it is not allowed to a virgin, but she is subjected in all things under the same condition, and the necessity of humility is reckoned to her along with the woman, whence will this one thing be allowed to her which is not allowed to every female? What prerogative does she deserve against her own condition, if she is a virgin and has proposed to sanctify her flesh? Is exemption from the veil granted her for this reason, so that she may enter the church notable and distinguished, so that she may display the honor of sanctity in the freedom of her head? She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office.

I know well that somewhere a virgin has been placed in the order of widows before the age of twenty. If the bishop owed her any refreshment, he could certainly have provided it in another way while preserving respect for discipline, so that such a miracle, I should not say monster, would not be marked out in the church: a virgin widow, all the more portentous because she did not cover her head even as a widow, denying both that she is a virgin who is counted as a widow, and that she is a widow who is called a virgin. But she sits there unveiled by the same authority as a virgin, and to that seat, beyond sixty years of age, not only married women are sometimes chosen, but also mothers, and indeed those who have raised children, so that, built up by experiences of all affections, they may easily know how to help other women with counsel and comfort, and so that they may have run through those things by which a woman can be tested. So nothing at all is permitted to a virgin for honor from that place.
notes: The source text contains a duplicated 'Potuit' at the start of the sentence 'Potuit Potuit dignius honorari...'; this appears to be a scribal dittography. The gloss renders it once.

problems.quote: Could she not be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?
problems.source_quote: Potuit Potuit dignius honorari aliqua praerogativa virilis aut gradus aut officii.
problems.why: English adds "not", reversing the Latin question’s meaning.
problems.fix: Could she be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?

problems.quote: Is the pardon of a veil granted to her for this
problems.why: 'venia' here means 'indulgence' or 'license' (concession), not 'pardon'; it is a concession to go unveiled.
problems.fix: Is the indulgence of a veil granted to her for this
problems.ruling: Latin 'velaminis venia' = permission/license, not 'pardon'; English misstates concession.

edits.old: Could she not be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?
edits.new: Could she be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?

edits.old: Is the pardon of a veil granted to her for this
edits.new: Is the indulgence of a veil granted to her for this

fixed: Negation: source 'Potuit Potuit dignius honorari aliqua praerogativa virilis aut gradus aut officii' has no negative; removed 'not'.
Mistranslation: source 'Idcirco velaminis venia fit illi' uses 'venia' as indulgence/license, not pardon; changed to 'indulgence'.

problems.quote: Is the indulgence of a veil granted to her for this
problems.why: This is a rhetorical question expecting 'no'; 'fit' here means 'is it made/granted' as a question, not a statement.
problems.fix: Is the indulgence of a veil made to her for this reason
problems.ruling: Idcirco velaminis venia fit illi is declarative; English makes it a question, altering the sense.

problems.why: 'praeter' here means 'beyond' (i.e., over sixty years old), not 'besides' (in addition to).
problems.ruling: praeter annos sexaginta means ‘beyond sixty years’; translation ‘besides sixty years’ misstates the age condition.

problems.why: English adds “once-” altering the meaning; Latin specifies married women, not widows or formerly married women.
problems.ruling: univirae means 'once-married women' (married only once); 'once-' is correct, not an addition. Claim is wrong.

edits.old: Is the indulgence of a veil granted to her for this
edits.new: Is the indulgence of a veil made to her for this reason

edits.old: not only once-married women, that is, married women

fixed: Changed 'granted' to 'made' and added 'reason' to match 'Idcirco velaminis venia fit illi' as a rhetorical question.
Changed 'besides' to 'beyond' to match 'praeter annos sexaginta' meaning 'over sixty years of age'.
Removed 'once-married' and the redundant gloss 'that is, married women' to match 'univirae, id est nuptae' which specifies married women, not formerly married women.

problems.quote: Is the indulgence of a veil made to her for this reason
problems.why: velaminis venia is leave to go unveiled, not the grant of a veil; the purpose clauses require that.
problems.fix: Is exemption from the veil granted her for this reason, so that she may enter the church conspicuous and distinguished and display the honor of sanctity by the freedom of her head?
problems.ruling: 'velaminis venia' is leave from the veil, since the purposes are 'in libertate capitis'. 'Indulgence of a veil... made to her' reads as being granted a veil, reversing the sense.

edits.old: Is the indulgence of a veil made to her for this reason
edits.new: Is exemption from the veil granted her for this reason

fixed: Fixed 'velaminis venia': 'Idcirco velaminis venia fit illi' with purpose clauses 'ut introeat... ut ostendat in libertate capitis' means leave to go unveiled, so 'indulgence of a veil' -> 'exemption from the veil'.

problems.quote: Could she be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?
problems.source_quote: Potuit Potuit dignius honorari aliqua praerogativa virilis aut gradus aut officii.
problems.why: Source is a statement: she could have been honored more worthily by some manly prerogative of rank or office, not a question. Mood and force changed.
problems.fix: She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office.
problems.ruling: 'Potuit ... honorari' is indicative assertion. English 'Could she...' makes it a question and changes force.

edits.old: Could she be honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office?
edits.new: She could have been honored more worthily by some prerogative of manly rank or office.

fixed: Fixed interrogative to declarative statement per source 'Potuit Potuit dignius honorari': indicative past potential, not a question.

polish.changed: Clarified 'offer the sacrifice' as 'offer the Eucharist' and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: placed in the order of widows before the age of twenty
notes.why: Reader may not know 'widows' is a church office, not just marital status.
notes.fix: Note that 'widows' designates an ordained church order of senior women.

notes.why: Reader may not know this refers to the Eucharist.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'nor to offer the Eucharistic sacrifice.'

polish.changed: I clarified the flow by separating the rhetorical questions from the discussion of the virgin widow, making the speaker's argument easier to follow, and I removed the duplicated 'Potuit' that appeared in the source text.

notes.why: Reader may not know this was a recognized church office for older women, not just a social category.
notes.fix: Note that the 'order of widows' was a recognized church office for elderly women of proven character.

last_rejected.quote: Is the indulgence of a veil made to her for this reason
last_rejected.why: Tertullian is being ironic: the veil is a concession, not an indulgence granted so she can show off unveiled.
last_rejected.fix: Is the concession of a veil made to her for this reason
last_rejected.ruling: ‘velaminis venia’ = permission/concession of a veil; “indulgence” is acceptable, irony not essential to meaning.

last_rejected.quote: But she sits there unveiled by the same authority as a virgin
last_rejected.source_quote: Sed ea auctoritate illic sedet intecta qua et virgo
last_rejected.why: Means 'by the same authority by which a virgin [sits]' — she claims virgin's authority while sitting as widow.
last_rejected.fix: But she sits there unveiled by the same authority as a virgin does
last_rejected.ruling: ‘intecta qua et virgo’ conveys sitting uncovered like a virgin; translation captures core sense despite nuance.

last_rejected.why: Latin "tinguere" means to dye/color, not to baptize; the English adds a sacramental act not in the source.
last_rejected.fix: nor to dye (or color) her hair
last_rejected.ruling: tinguere is Tertullian's standard term for baptize; see e.g. De Bapt. 4, 12, 15. Not a mistranslation.
